title: James Hardie Releases Annual Sustainability Report
summary: Company announces progress in building resilience through process integration, product innovation and strengthening communities.
body_text: SYDNEY & CHICAGO, August 25, 2025 - James Hardie Industries plc (ASX: JHX; NYSE: JHX), (“James Hardie” or the “Company”), a leader in providing high-performance, low-maintenance building products and solutions, and a company inspiring how communities design build and grow, today released its latest annual sustainability report entitled “Building Resilience.” “At James Hardie, sustainability is foundational to how we do business. We are continuing to make progress, evolve and innovate to ensure homes are built to last,” said Aaron Erter, Chief Executive Officer, James Hardie. “Sustainability is a journey, and this continues with our recent acquisition of The AZEK® Company in July 2025. As the industry leader in exterior home and outdoor living solutions, we have never been better positioned to explore a variety of ways we can improve our communities and our planet. At James Hardie, we are constantly working towards our purpose of Building a Better Future for All™ .” The report features initiatives to advance the company’s purpose and details progress across the four primary pillars of the company’s environmental, social and governance (ESG) strategy: Zero Harm, Planet, Innovation, and Communities. Highlights from the report for fiscal year 2025, include: Integration into Business Processes Sustainability strategies continue to be integrated into the Hardie Manufacturing Operating System (HMOS). The company set short-term internal natural gas targets for each region, helping drive the reduction of Scope 1+2 emissions by 14 percent in fiscal year 2025 from the calendar year 2021 baseline. Circular Supply Chain Efforts to reduce waste and create a circular supply chain for fiber cement products in North America plants diverted over 11 percent of manufacturing waste from local landfills in fiscal year 2025. In the Asia Pacific region, the company eliminated 98 percent of waste material sent to landfills by either recycling it back into production processes or sending it to local companies to keep waste materials in the value stream. Zero Harm Over a three-year period, the company is investing more than $75 million in strategic safety infrastructure projects globally. Safety standards for energy control processes, machine guarding, working from heights and electrical safety were developed and independently approved in North America and Asia Pacific. Product Innovation The company announced the TimberHue™ Collection in North America, featuring two-tone, premium finishes in eight authentic wood-look colors—engineered to withstand harsh weather and made with noncombustible* James Hardie technology. The Hardie™ Architectural Collection expanded to include Hardie® Artisan® Siding, featuring extra-thick lap boards and deep shadow lines for a natural wood aesthetic with the strength of fiber cement; also introduced Hardie® Architectural Panel, designed for vertical or horizontal installation to provide greater design flexibility, launching across North America in 2025. In Europe, fermacell® Therm25™, an easy-to-install fiber gypsum product, has lower CO2 emissions compared to conventional flooring and incorporates recycled gypsum, reducing landfill waste and reliance on mined materials. In the United States, Green Builder Media recognized James Hardie as an innovation and brand leader, naming Hardie® Artisan® Trim as a 2025 Sustainable Product of the Year. Respecting Human Rights The business launched a global human rights policy and completed the first salient issues review, conducting on-site social compliance audits of the few tier-one suppliers in high-risk environments. Stronger Workforce The launch of the BuildWell program is helping to create a culture of well-being, where employees are supported with education, resources and opportunities for their physical, mental, social and financial well-being, tailored to the specific needs of employees in different regions. Stronger Communities James Hardie contributed $1.65 billion in economic value to the communities in which it operates through capital expenditures at plants and by investing in employees, local ecosystems and across the supplier base. The company continued its global collaboration with Habitat for Humanity International®, and provided 29 Habitat Strong grants to build affordable and climate-resilient homes in fiscal year 2025. Integrating with The AZEK ® Company As announced in July 2025 , James Hardie successfully completed its previously announced acquisition of The AZEK® Company (“AZEK”). James Hardie now features a portfolio of high-performance, low-maintenance exterior and outdoor living brands, including Hardie®, TimberTech®, AZEK® Exteriors, Versatex®, fermacell®, StruXure®, Ultralox® and Intex®. AZEK® embeds sustainability into every stage of its operations, from material sourcing and manufacturing to product durability and end-of-life solutions. Guided by a full-circle approach, AZEK® transforms waste and scrap into high-performance, long-lasting materials and aims to incorporate one billion pounds of recycled content into its manufacturing annually. Its latest sustainability report highlighting progress toward environmental and recycling initiatives during AZEK®’s fiscal 2024 is available here . “As we continue to integrate with AZEK®, we are harnessing our collective strengths to advance our sustainability leadership and position the combined company for even greater impact. This work is shaping the next generation of our sustainability goals, and we look forward to sharing more on this important topic in the future,” said Amanda Cimaglia, Vice President, Global Sustainability, James Hardie. Building Resilience James Hardie’s sustainability goals align directly with issues that matter most to its stakeholders and overall corporate objectives. The company’s sustainability strategy is driven through cross-functional collaboration, including research and development, engineering, manufacturing, finance and human resources leadership. In fiscal year 2023, the company adopted new, more ambitious sustainability goals to help track and assess progress. In fiscal year 2024, the company set near-term regional targets that roll up to overall longer-term goals. Each regional president is held accountable for attaining these targets in the region and is provided funding in the regional budget to support initiatives at the local level. As a result, the entire organization is engaged in and committed to these goals. *Hardie® siding complies with ASTM E136 as a noncombustible material. For more information about James Hardie Building Products Inc., visit www.jameshardie.com . About James Hardie James Hardie Industries plc (NYSE: JHX; ASX: JHX) is the industry leader in exterior home and outdoor living solutions, with a portfolio that includes fiber cement, fiber gypsum, and composite and PVC decking and railing products. Products offered by James Hardie are engineered for beauty, durability, and climate resilience, and include trusted brands like Hardie®, TimberTech®, AZEK® Exteriors, Versatex®, fermacell® and StruXure®. With a global footprint, James Hardie products are marketed and sold throughout North America, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region. James Hardie Industries plc is a limited liability company incorporated in Ireland with its registered office at 1st Floor, Block A, One Park Place, Upper Hatch Street, Dublin 2, D02 FD79, Ireland. For more information and media resources, visit JamesHardie.com/about-us/media resources./about-us/media-resources . For investor information, please visit ir.jameshardie.com.au . title: Keep your air conditioner working when you need it most | Black Hills Energy
body_text: Keep your air conditioner working when you need it most When temperatures rise, your air conditioner becomes one of the hardest working systems in your home. And when it’s under that kind of strain, even small issues can quickly turn into bigger, more expensive problems. That’s something Kevin sees every day. As one of our Colorado Service Guard technicians, Kevin is often the one homeowners rely on when something stops working. In his experience, many of the issues he repairs could have been minimized, or even avoided, with a few simple habits. Kevin’s simple at-home air conditioner maintenance tips A little routine care can go a long way. Here are a few simple steps Kevin recommends: Change your air filter regularly Swap out filters every 30–60 days, especially during heavy-use months. A clean filter keeps air moving and reduces strain on your system. Keep vents open and clear Closing vents or blocking them with furniture can disrupt airflow and make your system work harder than it should. Check your return vents Make sure nothing is covering return vents — restricted airflow can impact performance across your entire system. Give your outdoor unit some space Leaves, dirt and debris can build up around the condenser. Keeping it clear helps your A/C run more efficiently. Even small actions like these can help improve performance and reduce wear and tear on your air conditioner. When appliance breakdowns happen, you’re covered Even with good maintenance, A/C systems can still break down — especially during periods of heavy use in the heat of summer. title: The Marketing Automation Software Audit: 9 Questions to Ask Before You Renew
summary: These 9 questions are part of a vendor-agnostic audit with clear pass and fail criteria, so you can recommit with confidence or move on with a plan.
body_text: Your renewal date is the one moment when the vendor relationship tilts back in your favor. Before you sign, you hold leverage you won't have again for another year or two. Instead of clicking auto-renew and inheriting last year's limitations, you should be treating your renewal as a checkpoint. The nine questions below form a vendor-agnostic audit with clear pass and fail criteria, so you can recommit with confidence or move on with a plan. Why the renewal moment matters Marketing automation in 2026 means more than scheduling batch sends. Automation now runs on trigger-based workflows where a customer action starts a chain of personalized responses across channels, as one leading marketing platform describes it. The gap between a platform that simply schedules messages and one that acts on live behavior is where most teams feel friction. That friction usually surfaces at renewal. You've spent a year working around the tool's blind spots, and now you're being asked to pay for another year of the same. A structured audit turns that frustration into a decision framework. Run each question against your current platform, mark it pass or fail, and let the tally guide your next move. 1. Does our platform truly support every channel our customers use? This is the starting point because customer attention today has never been more scattered. A person might tap a push notification in the morning, open an email at lunch, and respond to an SMS at night. A platform's job is to unify those moments inside one workflow, not add a new login for each one. What a good answer looks like: A single interface where you build a cross-channel journey that branches across push notifications, email, SMS, RCS, in-app messages, and Live Activities based on user behavior. Adding a new channel should not require buying a new tool. This is the practical difference between a true multi-channel messaging platform and a stack of disconnected point solutions. The distinction matters. Your messaging should bring disparate channels into a single continuous conversation, keeping context and history intact regardless of which channel the customer uses, while instead of operating in silos that force customers to repeat themselves. A capable platform supports multiple channels from one interface, including mobile push, web push, email, SMS/RCS, in-app messages, and Live Activities, all managed through a single setup flow where email and SMS can be configured without a developer. Red flags: You log into separate systems for different channels, you rely on brittle integrations to stitch services together, or you discover mid-campaign that the platform doesn't support a channel your audience actually uses. Audit your own user behavior before you talk to any vendor so you know exactly which channels to require. 2. Can we orchestrate complex lifecycle journeys without engineering help? A not so fun fact: speed dies when every campaign needs a developer ticket. If your marketers can't build, test, and launch on their own, the platform is a bottleneck rather than an accelerator. This question sits at the heart of lifecycle marketing, where the value comes from reacting quickly at each stage. What a good answer looks like: A visual, drag-and-drop journey builder that a non-technical marketer can use to create multi-step onboarding, re-engagement, and win-back flows triggered by user behavior. The fundamentals of a good automated campaign come down to collecting data, setting up segments, and targeting users at key milestones. A capable platform gives marketers a visual canvas to automate multi-channel flows without writing code. Map your platform against the full lifecycle. Onboarding should activate new users. Activation flows should drive the first habit-forming action. Retention journeys should reward continued use. Win-back sequences should re-engage lapsed users before they churn for good. A capable platform automates all four; a limited one covers one or two and leaves the rest manual. Red flags: The UI requires custom scripting for basic branching logic, or the workflow builder is so dense that only a couple of specialists can touch it. If launching a simple two-step flow means opening a project ticket, your team's agility is capped. 3. How quickly does our platform act on real-time user data? "Real-time" is one of the most abused words in this category. This question forces the vendor to define it. Personalization depends on speed: when a shopper abandons a cart, the follow-up needs to land in minutes, not the next morning. What a good answer looks like: A new user event, a purchase, a feature use, a page view, becomes available for segmentation and targeting in single-digit minutes. That latency is what lets you build segments from real-time engagement and reach people while intent is still fresh. A capable platform lets you create highly relevant campaigns based on real-time user engagement and connect that data to personalized messages using attributes, events, location, and language. Red flags: The platform relies on 24-hour batch syncs, or "real-time" segments actually take several hours to update. Either one kills in-session marketing and turns your abandoned-cart flow into an afterthought that arrives too late to matter. 4. How deeply does it integrate with our core tech stack? Your automation platform doesn't operate alone. It has to read from and write to your CDP, analytics tools, CRM, and data warehouse. Weak integration creates data silos and blocks the unified customer view that makes personalization possible. What a good answer looks like: Native, pre-built connections to leading analytics platforms , major CDPs, and data warehouses, plus a well-documented REST API for custom needs. When you evaluate a vendor, ask specifically how data flows in and out of the platform and what CRM integrations they provide, which one marketing technology evaluation checklist lists as the first questions to raise. Red flags: The vendor offers only basic webhooks, requires expensive custom development for core connections, or can't read your existing systems without a major engineering project. If integration is a professional-services line item, factor that into your renewal math. 5. Is our reporting actionable, or just a data dump? The question isn't whether the platform has a dashboard. It's whether the analytics help you make better decisions. Good reporting attributes lift and retention to specific campaigns and channels so you know what's working. What a good answer looks like: You can track conversions, measure channel-specific lift across retention cohorts, and follow a user's journey through multiple channels. You can share insights with stakeholders without needing a data scientist to translate them. Reporting should be customizable, and you should be able to confirm the platform actually measures success against your goals rather than just counting activity. Red flags: Reports show only vanity metrics like sends and opens, lack cohort analysis, or can't connect a conversion back to the cross-channel path that produced it. If you can't answer "which campaign drove this retention lift," the reporting is decorative. 6. What's the true total cost of ownership for the next year? The base subscription is rarely the real number. Overages, per-seat licenses, and support tiers can double an invoice. Renewal is your chance to scrutinize the full total cost of ownership before you commit. What a good answer looks like: Transparent, predictable pricing. Ask the vendor a direct set of questions: Is pricing based on users, events, or sends? What are the overage penalties, and how have they hit past invoices? Are there extra fees for seats, support, or API access? Does the model scale predictably as your audience and team grow? The switching-cost question is also part of the calculation. Weigh the true cost of migrating against the cost of staying, including retraining, data migration, and the productivity dip during transition. A pricing model that scales cleanly, where usage grows with your business rather than penalizing headcount, keeps that math simple. Red flags: Vague pricing tiers and surprise overage charges on prior bills. If you can't forecast next year's spend within a reasonable range, that's a renewal risk. 7. How portable is our data if we decide to leave? Your user data is one of your most valuable assets. A confident, customer-friendly vendor makes it easy to leave; a nervous one makes it hard. This question tests both data ownership and the vendor's good faith. Red flags: The vendor is evasive about export, the process requires paid professional services, or contract clauses make extraction slow or incomplete. Data you can't retrieve is data you don't really control. 8. What's the vendor's product roadmap, and does it align with ours? You aren't renewing for the platform as it exists today. You're renewing for what it becomes over the next contract term. Treat this as a partnership question. AI decisioning and real-time data activation are widely cited as the top differentiating capabilities for 2026 platforms. If your vendor isn't investing there, ask why. Red flags: No public-facing roadmap, infrequent and minor updates, or development priorities aimed at a vertical that isn't yours. A vendor building for a different market will drift away from your needs over time. 9. What level of support, security, and compliance can we expect? When something breaks at 2 a.m. during a campaign send, support quality is everything. And with data regulation expanding, compliance is non-negotiable. Break this final question into three parts. Support: Ask about response-time commitments, whether phone support exists, its hours, and whether a dedicated account manager comes with your tier. Security: Ask for a summary of third-party audit reports and certifications. A vendor confident in its security practices will share this readily. Compliance: Ask directly about support for GDPR , CCPA , and any regional data protection laws you're subject to. Review the vendor's data processing documentation. A thorough Data Protection Addendum should describe the provider's third-party audit and certification programs, make summary audit reports available on request, and define the customer's own audit rights. Red flags: No SLA on support response, no certifications to show, or evasiveness on regional compliance. Any of these should stall a renewal until you get straight answers. Time for a change of scenery? If you ran this audit and your current platform came up short, it might be time to see what you've been missing. body_text: Key Takeaways For subscription SaaS, the real ROI of AR automation is churn reduction and upsell lift — not the labor savings most calculators stop at. Automated AR cuts Days Sales Outstanding by 8 to 15 days versus manual processing. Cash application drops from €4-8 per transaction by hand to under €0.50 automated. Automated systems match payments at rates above 95%, killing most reconciliation errors. At €100M revenue, every single day you cut from DSO frees roughly €274,000 in working capital. Labor cost avoidance runs €17,500 to €37,500 a month for a business processing 5,000 payments monthly. Churn and upsell are the hardest numbers to calculate — 1 to 2 days each, versus hours for a payback period. Quick Summary For subscription SaaS, the ROI of AR automation comes down to two numbers your competitors almost never calculate: churn reduction and upsell lift . Faster, cleaner billing keeps subscribers from cancelling over payment friction. That retention math dwarfs the labor savings most calculators stop at. Compare accounts receivable automation vs. traditional manual processes and the operational wins are immediate. Automation speeds the collection cycle, fixes payment matching, and cuts transaction costs. For recurring-revenue businesses, that efficiency feeds straight into retention. Which ROI methods actually matter for SaaS The useful methods measure both operational savings and revenue protection. Here’s how the main approaches stack up. Method What It Measures Time to Calculate Difficulty SaaS-Specific Value Payback period Months to recover automation cost 1-2 hours Easy Fast go/no-go signal DSO reduction Working capital freed per day cut Half a day Medium ~€274K enable per DSO day at €100M revenue Labor cost avoidance Manual hours removed 2-3 hours Easy €17,500-37,500/month saved at 5,000 payments/month Churn reduction Subscribers retained via smoother billing 1-2 days Hard Recovers involuntary churn from failed cards Upsell lift Expansion revenue from self-service portals 1-2 days Hard Frees AR team for account growth work What realistic payback looks like Most SaaS firms recover their automation investment inside the first few months. A Billtrust ROI study found 93% of finance leaders confirmed their AR automation delivered the expected return, and 100% reported measurable gains like faster payments and lower costs. The working capital math is concrete. A company at €200M revenue can release €5.48M from a 10-day DSO improvement. That’s cash you push into product or sales instead of chasing invoices. On timing: AI-native AR tools deploy in 4-8 weeks . Legacy systems drag out to 3-6 months . For subscription firms, faster deployment means the churn-reduction clock starts sooner. Why churn and upsell belong in the formula Skip the churn calculation only if you bill one-off invoices with no recurring relationship. For everyone running subscriptions, involuntary churn from expired cards and failed retries is a silent revenue leak. Automated dunning and card updates plug it directly. Research on AI-driven AR shows a 35% faster collection cycle and a 75% cut in manual follow-up effort . That reclaimed capacity is the hidden upsell engine. When collectors aren’t chasing overdue accounts, they run expansion conversations instead. Add it up. Labor savings pay for the tool. Churn reduction and upsell lift are what turn AR automation into a growth investment instead of a cost cut. That’s the calculation to run before you sign anything. Why this isn’t just about saving a few hours For subscription SaaS, the case for automating AR isn’t about clawing back staff time. It’s about keeping revenue you already won. Payment friction is a quiet churn driver, and manual billing generates plenty of it. The gap between automation and manual processes shows up most clearly in how customers experience getting billed. Manual workflows mean late invoices, mismatched payments, and dunning emails that go out days after a card fails. For recurring revenue, every one of those errors is a reason for a subscriber to walk. How much do manual AR tasks actually cost? Manual AR eats staff hours that scale badly with invoice volume. Automation drops cash application labor to a fraction of the manual cost while handling 60-80% of routine collections without a human touching it. A growing company running thousands of recurring transactions can wipe out hundreds of hours of manual data entry, which turns into real monthly payroll savings. But the follow-up burden matters more than the payroll line. Finance teams running manual collections spend roughly a third of their week on repetitive chasing. Cut that, and your team isn’t hounding customers who already churned over a billing mistake nobody caught in time. What automation fixes that manual work can’t Automation removes the errors that erode trust. 52% of CFOs at highly automated firms reported fewer mistakes in invoicing and payment processing. For a subscriber, a clean invoice and an instant payment confirmation are part of the product experience. Three problems get solved directly: Billing errors that trigger disputes. Vision language models hit 99.7% extraction accuracy on structured remittance data, so payments match invoices without manual keying. Slow collections that strand cash. Automated dunning recovers a meaningful share of failed charges within the first retry window, freeing working capital you can redeploy. Failed-payment friction. Automatic reminders and reconciliation catch involuntary churn before a lapsed card cancels a subscription. That last point is where the SaaS math diverges from generic AR advice. A failed renewal caught automatically is a retained subscriber. The same failed renewal caught three weeks later by an overworked clerk is often a cancellation. Who gets the biggest return High-volume, recurring-revenue businesses. SaaS firms bill the same customers over and over, so every reduction in payment friction compounds across the customer lifetime, not just a single transaction. The retention math backs this up. Involuntary churn from failed payments makes up a large slice of total SaaS churn, and automated retry logic recovers a sizable portion of those at-risk accounts before they lapse. Every recovered renewal protects the full remaining lifetime value of that subscriber, not one invoice. And the reframe competitors miss: a faster collection cycle doesn’t just improve cash flow. It shortens the window where a billing problem can push someone toward cancellation, and it frees the same customer-facing team to run upsell conversations instead of collections calls. That retention and expansion lift is the number that dwarfs the labor savings. Calculating the cost of manual collections The true cost of manual collections is three buckets: labor, materials, and opportunity cost. The third bucket is where the real damage hides. Every delayed dunning cycle risks a subscriber cancelling, so your formula has to price in lost recurring revenue, not just staff hours. This is exactly where the automation-versus-manual comparison gets misjudged. Most calculators stop at labor. Run the two models honestly for a recurring-revenue business and the opportunity cost of a slow, error-prone manual process outweighs the payroll line by a wide margin. The formula for total manual collections cost Total cost of manual collections = labor cost + materials cost + opportunity cost (delayed payments and churned revenue). Labor covers the staff hours spent chasing payments and applying cash. Materials cover printing, postage, and per-transaction processing. Opportunity cost covers the working capital trapped by high DSO plus the recurring revenue you lose when payment friction pushes subscribers out. Run all three. Skip one and you undercount the case for automation. Estimating labor costs Labor is the biggest visible line. Manual cash application is notoriously expensive per transaction, while automated systems process the same payments for pennies. A team manually processing 2,500 payments a month at a €7 blended cost is spending €17,500 monthly just to apply cash and follow up. Then add the hidden drag: manual cash application carries error rates that force teams to spend 20 to 30 minutes reworking each misapplied payment, and a 2% mismatch rate across those transactions means dozens of exceptions a month eating another full week of staff time. For a SaaS firm, those freed hours matter twice. Your AR staff stop rekeying invoices and start resolving the billing disputes that actually make subscribers leave. What materials and opportunity costs add Materials are the smaller bucket: paper invoices, postage, per-document processing. The bigger hit is opportunity cost, and for subscription businesses it splits in two. Working capital cost. Manual workflows carry DSO that runs 20 to 30% higher than automated ones. Each day of DSO reduction frees substantial capital otherwise locked in unpaid invoices. For a mid-market firm, that liquidity can easily hit six figures per day cut. Cash stuck in receivables can’t fund your next upsell push. Churned revenue cost. This is the line competitors ignore. A failed card that sits three days before a dunning email goes out is a live cancellation risk. Multiply your involuntary churn rate by average contract value and you’ll see manual collections quietly bleeding recurring revenue every month. Case study: cutting collection costs through automation One mid-market company moved off manual collections and hit 23% ROI within six months . It cut manual invoice entry by half and improved DSO from 45 days to 30 days . That 15-day swing did two things at once. It released working capital fast, and it tightened the billing experience so customers needed far fewer follow-ups. The controller reported a sharp drop in payment follow-ups after the switch. For a SaaS firm, fewer follow-ups mean fewer friction points, and fewer friction points mean fewer cancellations. That’s the retention math your manual process has been quietly costing you. Step-by-step ROI calculation To calculate AR automation ROI for a subscription business, you plug two SaaS-specific gains into the standard formula: retained recurring revenue and upsell lift. Most calculators ignore both. The base formula stays simple. ROI = (Net Benefits − Cost of Implementation) / Cost of Implementation × 100 . What separates automation from manual processing in this math is what you count as a benefit. Manual-process calculators stop at labor savings. For a subscription firm, you add churn reduction and upsell revenue on top. What you need before you start Gather five baseline inputs from your current manual workflow: annual recurring revenue, monthly involuntary churn rate, DSO, cash application cost per transaction, and staff hours spent chasing payments. That’s your “before” picture. Automation ROI is only credible measured against a documented baseline. Companies that run a proper process assessment first see 25-40% higher ROI than those who skip it. So do the boring part. Pull real figures, not estimates. A worked example Take a SaaS firm with €10M ARR , a 1.5% monthly involuntary churn rate driven by failed cards and late dunning, and a manual AR team processing 5,000 payments per month at €6 per transaction . Step 1: Labor savings. Automation drops cash application from €6 to under €0.50 . That’s a swing of roughly €27,500 per month , or €330,000 annually . This is the number generic calculators report, then stop. Step 2: Churn reduction. Faster automated dunning and card-retry logic cut involuntary churn. Recover even a third of that 1.5% monthly leak and you retain roughly 0.5% of ARR per month . On €10M ARR, that’s about €50,000 in monthly recurring revenue saved , or €600,000 a year . This dwarfs the labor line. Step 3: Upsell lift. Clean billing and self-service payment portals free your finance team to support expansion instead of firefighting. Redirect a few reclaimed hours per week toward accounts ready to upgrade and the effect compounds. Assign a conservative €120,000 annual upsell lift here. Step 4: Total it up. Net benefits = €330,000 + €600,000 + €120,000 = €1,050,000 . If the platform costs €150,000 to implement and run for the year, your ROI is: (€1,050,000 − €150,000) / €150,000 × 100 = 600%. Strip out churn and upsell and that same calculation drops to 120%. The retention effect is where the real return lives. What skews the numbers The most common error is counting only labor savings and ignoring recovered recurring revenue. For a subscription firm, that undercounts ROI by a wide margin. The second mistake is treating ROI as a one-time figure. Monitor it quarterly. Recovery rates shift as card-retry logic tunes itself and dunning sequences mature, so a figure that looks flat at month three often climbs by month nine. Mid-market firms often hit rapid payback, and a phased rollout gets you there faster with 30-50% fewer configuration changes . Bake churn and upsell into every review. Skip them and you’ll systematically undervalue what automation does for a recurring-revenue business. Benchmarking ROI: industry standards and metrics To benchmark your AR automation ROI, compare against three industry numbers: first-year ROI, adoption satisfaction, and Days to Pay reduction. Research on intelligent automation across 247 organizations in 15 industries found an average ROI of 30% to 300% , with a median of 150% in the first year . That’s your baseline. If you’re a subscription firm, you should beat it, because retention lift stacks on top of the labor savings those numbers already capture. This is the blind spot in most automation-versus-manual comparisons. Cross-industry benchmarks blend AR in with accounts payable and reconciliation, so the reported figure reflects a general-ledger average, not a collections-specific one. For recurring-revenue businesses, that averaging undercounts the payback. The generic benchmark measures faster cash and lower cost. It ignores the subscriber you keep because their card retry succeeded and the dunning email never went out. What benchmarks SaaS firms should track Benchmark against three metrics: first-year ROI, expected-ROI hit rate, and Days to Pay improvement. Industry surveys show the vast majority of finance executives find their automated systems meet or exceed the targets set during planning, with reported error-rate drops on invoicing and cash application running into double digits. Those are the floor numbers. A subscription firm layers two more on top. Track your gross revenue retention before and after automation, and your upsell conversion rate on accounts with clean billing histories. Neither shows up in a standard calculator, and both move your true ROI well past the ceiling the cross-industry data reports. Two structural factors widen the gap. Cloud-based deployments generate 25% higher returns than on-premises setups. And companies with standardized processes achieve roughly 30% higher returns than those running fragmented workflows. For SaaS teams already in the cloud with structured billing data, both tailwinds are baked in. How first-party collections ROI compares First-party collections ROI comes from keeping the customer relationship intact while automating the follow-up. For subscription businesses, a gentler, faster, automated dunning sequence preserves the relationship you’d otherwise strain with aggressive manual chasing. Speed alone isn’t the win; the retained account is. In-house collections carry real hidden costs. Labor scales badly with volume, and every new hire needs training on your billing edge cases. Automation handles the vast majority of routine collections work, freeing your team from the repetitive follow-ups that burn hours and goodwill. One documented example makes the point. An AI collections assistant deployed at a large professional-services firm cut the accounts receivable period by roughly 22% . Another organization saved over 15,000 staff hours per month and halved document turnaround times. Those savings are real, but for a SaaS firm the retention effect that clean, prompt collections produces is what pushes your benchmarked ROI past the industry median. Where your numbers should land Aim to beat the standard benchmarks. If your automated collections recover the bulk of aging invoices before they hit 60 days past due and your write-off rate trends toward the low single digits, you’re pacing with top performers. Then check the two SaaS metrics competitors skip: is gross retention up, and are clean-billing accounts converting to upsells faster? That’s where your real ROI separates from the generic benchmark. Frequently Asked Questions 1. What is involuntary churn and why does it matter for AR automation ROI? Involuntary churn happens when subscribers lapse due to expired cards, failed payments, or delayed retries—not because they chose to leave. It represents a large slice of total SaaS churn. Automated dunning and card-update logic recover these accounts before cancellation, protecting the full remaining lifetime value of each subscriber. 2. How does cloud-based AR automation compare to on-premises deployment for ROI? Cloud-based AR automation deployments deliver significantly stronger returns than on-premises setups. Cloud systems also deploy faster and integrate more easily with structured billing data. For SaaS teams already operating in the cloud with standardized workflows, this operational advantage is built in from day one. 3. How often should I recalculate my AR automation ROI after implementation? Recalculate AR automation ROI quarterly rather than treating it as a one-time figure. Recovery rates shift as card-retry logic tunes itself and dunning sequences mature. A figure that looks flat at month three often climbs by month nine, so quarterly reviews capture the true, growing return. 4. Does AR automation ever make sense for businesses without recurring revenue? AR automation still benefits one-off invoicing businesses through labor savings, faster DSO, and highly accurate payment matching. However, you can skip the churn calculation entirely if you bill without recurring relationships. The retention and upsell math that drives the biggest returns applies mainly to subscription models. 5. What is a process assessment and why should I do one before automating? A process assessment documents your current manual workflow baseline—labor costs, DSO, error rates, and staff hours—before deploying automation. Companies that complete a proper assessment first achieve substantially stronger returns because they can target specific inefficiencies. Pull real figures rather than estimates for credible before-and-after comparisons. 6. How much staff time can AR automation actually reclaim? AR automation absorbs the vast majority of routine collections work and dramatically reduces manual follow-up effort. Leading implementations have demonstrated the ability to reclaim thousands of staff hours per month while halving document turnaround times. This reclaimed capacity lets finance teams shift from chasing overdue accounts to running expansion and upsell conversations. 7. What error rate should I expect from automated payment matching? Automated systems achieve exceptionally high payment match rates, utilizing advanced extraction models to read structured remittance data. This sharply reduces reconciliation errors. By comparison, manual cash application carries frequent mismatch rates, forcing teams to spend significant time manually investigating and reworking each misapplied payment.

title: Behind the Daunting Preparation for the 2026 Mille Miglia
summary: Completing the Mille Miglia is an act of extreme endurance. 1000 miles on north and central Italian roads, all open to the public, it used to be a race that saw competitors hit speeds of over 190 mph. The record running was a famously improbable 10 hours, 7 minutes, and 48 seconds set by Stirling […]
body_text: Completing the Mille Miglia is an act of extreme endurance. 1000 miles on north and central Italian roads, all open to the public, it used to be a race that saw competitors hit speeds of over 190 mph. The record running was a famously improbable 10 hours, 7 minutes, and 48 seconds set by Stirling Moss and Denis Jenkinson in 1955, averaging more than 97 mph. Two years later, following a deadly crash in Guidizzolo when the Ferrari 335S driven by Alfonso de Portago blew a tire and cartwheeled into spectators, the race was cancelled amid a massive public outcry and all motor racing on public roads was banned by the Italian government. In 1977, the race saw its second life start as the Mille Miglia Storico, a regularity race featuring cars of the exact make and model that competed in the original races. Today, it’s known simply by most as the 1000 Miglia, and has earned its place as one of the world’s most important historic motoring events. John Mayhead It’s still an endurance event, and in some ways more so than the original. Now roughly 1200 miles, the route is completed in five days and varies each year but retains the spirit of the original. After starting in Brescia, this year the competitors visited Padua before heading southwest across the Apennines to Montecatini Terme, through Rome, then back up to Rimini before crossing back in a figure eight to the finish back in Brescia. The route is navigated with a tulip-style logbook issued daily, without street names and with over 100 time trials along the way. Successful completion relies on extraordinary levels of concentration and communication between the navigator and driver with little more than an odometer and a trip computer to help. One of the greatest challenges in the modern event is the selection process that often starts years before. First, the purchase of a qualifying car of the correct make, model, and year that must be inspected by the owner’s national historic automobile organization to ensure it is all original and correct, then issued with the all-important FIVA (Fédération Internationale des Véhicules Anciens) passport. Next, the owner must sign up on the 1000 Miglia Registro, send in paperwork and photographs, pay just over €900, and wait. John Mayhead John Mayhead John Mayhead This is where the process becomes difficult. Questions are fired back and forth about the car: what’s been restored, is it an exact replica of the original, how can you prove this supercharger or that differential ratio was used in period? Once answered to the satisfaction of the organizers, there are two routes that ensure entry: those cars that took part in the original pre-1957 race, and the drivers who have won one of the warm-up events run by the 1000 Miglia team are both guaranteed starting places. The rest must apply and hope: there are roughly 1000 applicants every year for around 400 places, which includes those already guaranteed entry and the entries allocated to sponsors. Once that bar is cleared, then there are the costs, which can be significant. The standard, four-night package that includes hotels on the road, meals, mechanic passes and some gifts costs just under €16,000 including tax; the silver package, offering accommodation for two additional nights and uprated gifts, costs around €18,600; the gold package at around €22,000 offers six nights’ accommodation in two separate rooms. Then there’s shipping the car to Italy, the preparation of the car and the mechanical support on the road: although the organizers provide some, most opt for dedicated support. With flights, hotels before and after the event and other incidental costs, the total bill can easily reach €100,000 (about $114K as of this writing). Yet even after that investment, there is no guarantee of finishing; the physical toll on cars that are, in most cases, more than 70 years old is immense. To achieve that end, you need a team of superb, dedicated engineers and people with local knowledge combined with a sense of presence to overcome the inevitable Italian bureaucracy. This is the point at which Andrea Rizza enters stage left. He has that presence: imagine the archetypal Roman gladiator: tall, chiseled face, dark hair, dark eyes. I met Andrea at Salon Privé, the preeminent British concours that takes place annually at Blenheim Palace near Oxford, where we’re both judges. He is head of Rizza Classic, the historic department of Carrozzeria Rizza, a family business formed in 1949 and today run by father Alberto and son Andrea, with his brothers Mirko and Daniele, that specializes in the restoration and maintenance of historic cars to an exceptional level. He’s also a pragmatist: He knows that cars need to be well prepared, regularly driven, and their drivers need time behind the wheel. If you want your car to start, and more importantly finish the Mille Miglia, Andrea is the guy to know. A few years ago, when contracted to support another company, he realized he could do it better than the rest. John Mayhead John Mayhead At the same time, on the other side of the Atlantic, John Houghtaling and Franco Valobra were in search of a new challenge. From 1999 onwards, they’d been leading a thriving Ferrari racing scene in New Orleans that had grown into the Challenge Car Racing Championship (CCR), fielding races with up to 42 cars on the grid for twelve races per season, making them one of the biggest privateer Ferrari groups in the world. John Mayhead “When it started, we were just a group of guys with old Challenge Ferraris who wanted to race; we used to get the cops to shut the road, race up and down for a bit, then we’d stop and they’d let the traffic go,” Houghtaling told me. These early races, styled as the French Quarter Classic, started to gain a country-wide reputation and the social aspect grew; families were involved from the start. The word spread, and others were approached directly. John Herlihy bought a 360 Challenge, the first racing Ferrari he’d owned. “I asked him what he intended to do with it,” his wife, Julie told me. “He didn’t really have an answer.” Then Houghtaling rang, and Herlihy was in the club. By 2016, it was a successful non-profit, having a $20M+ impact on local good causes, but Houghtaling and Valobra had their sights set on the Mille Miglia. They bought the ex-Walt Hansgen Jaguar XK120M, a car with a stack of competition history that should be a dead-certain entry to the 1000-mile Italian race, but they didn’t get a place: there were already enough XK120s on the list. John Mayhead John Mayhead “We’d spent all this money on the car and the entry,” Houghtaling told me. “We just couldn’t find a way around it.” Then, speaking to the Mille Miglia team one day, he was given a lifeline when they told him many places were reserved for the cars of sponsors. He rang Franco. “What would you say if I could get you entry to the Mille Miglia as a sponsor?” he asked. It was a simple question to answer. Their social media company themanualshift.com was accepted as a sponsor by the Mille Miglia organizers with five entries per year included in the price. Taking one slot for themselves, they offered the others to their Ferrari-racing friends, with the suggestion that they source and prepare all five cars together to the same standard, with the attention to detail extending to period racing overalls and helmets. Ken Marlin was one of those who received the call. “John rang me and asked me whether I wanted to drive the Mille Miglia. I told him I had many questions, all under the heading of ‘yes’. My first was where do I wire the money?” John Herlihy shared the car with Ken, with Bruce Roch and his son Harrison in the third car, Chris Fountas and his friend Walter in the fourth, and two other friends of Houghtaling in the final Jaguar. Manual Shift Motorsports was founded. John Mayhead John Mayhead John Mayhead Then, in 2018, the two automotive worlds collided. Houghtaling and Valobra met Andrea, and were impressed by his ability, as he was of them, finishing as the second-highest-placed U.S. team. By 2022, Rizza had taken over all the Italian administration, booking a week-long build-up event that mixed the best hotels and moonlit dinners next to the impossibly beautiful Lake Garda with top-grade competition preparation, both mechanical and bureaucratic. If there was a problem with the car or the entry paperwork, Andrea’s crew fixed it, fast. John Mayhead This year, Andrea invited me to Italy to be part of the week-long preparation for the race, and to watch the start. The Manual Shift crew are old hands now: I asked John Herlihy, now representing the pre-war crowd with his 1937 BMW 328 partnered by his wife Julie, how many 1000 Miglias he’d completed. “Seven… maybe eight,” he replied, and it is extraordinary that so many of the original lineup are still active: this year, the two Johns and Franco were again joined by Ken, Chris, and Bruce. Although Jaguars are still well represented in the expanded group, some of the group have moved back to their first love of Ferrari: Houghtaling drove his 121 LM Spyder Scaglietti, the car in which Piero Taruffi was leading in 1955 before the oil pump ruptured, Valobra an exquisite 1955 750 Monza and Ken Marlin in his 1952 212/225S Sport Vignale Berlinetta, one of just two built with the stiffer Tuboscocca competition chassis. This isn’t just an aesthetic choice, either: The 121LM and the 225S both competed in the race before 1957, so both are automatically eligible, and these cars all have a higher coefficient, the number allocated by the organisers for age and historic importance to the race that is used to shade the final score, than the XK120s. 1952 212/225S Sport Vignale Berlinetta John Mayhead But despite the experience within the group, the need for such a shakedown before the race is still obvious. Daniele Rizza, brother of Andrea, told me about the endurance upgrades to the cars—improved fuel and brake lines, uprated cooling and batteries, suspension set up for the bumpy Italian roads—and then I followed as he took Marlin’s Ferrari to a registration office to gain a necessary piece of paper that would have, undoubtedly, failed to materialize for lesser mortals. Later, I drove to an underground garage in the center of Brescia where Andrea and one of his mechanics were dismantling the rear differential of the BMW, watched with great concern by Herlihy. Soon, they identified the problem: the pinion had disintegrated through age, dropping five teeth into the sump of the rear axle. The whole lot needed to be rebuilt in 24 hours prior to scrutineering. They made it, of course. A replacement crown and pinion was sourced from their workshop in Rome and driven up to Brescia overnight. Then, the car moved to the workshop of an old colleague, and the team set about stripping, cleaning and rebuilding the axle. The bearings were rebuilt, gaskets cut, and the new crown and pinion fitted, but even that came with its own complications as it had a slightly different gear ratio than the original, so Herlihy and Rizza’s team had to factor in how that affected speed and performance. Later, not far from Brescia at a Porsche Experience Centre, we watched as Chris Fountas calibrated his trip computer for the timed regularity (PC or Prove Cronometrate ) phases of the race, when cars must drive a set distance within a fraction of a second of the target time. John Mayhead The following day was Sunday, two days before the start of the race. In convoy, the cars left the grand Villa Cortine Palace hotel in the old town of Sirmione, the picturesque spit at the southern shore of Lake Garda, and made their way into Brescia, about 45 minutes distant. There, in a huge, modern expo center, the cars were inspected by the scrutineers and finally awarded their official race roundels showing their start number. That night, we returned to Sirmione for dinner and almost took over a restaurant, the group now having been swollen by more family and friends who had come to offer support. The following day, it was back again, this time for the official sealing parade when the cars are fitted with their traditional wire around the steering column fixed with a lead seal, the mark of a very special car. The stickers may disappear from a car over time; the lead seals very rarely do. That night, the group moved to the Villa Biondelli in the Franciacorta wine region closer to Brescia. From here, it was a 30-minute drive to the Viale Venezia, a tree-lined road on the outskirts of the town that hosts the starting line. There, you gain the first real concept of how large the event is: not just the 430 entrant cars from pre-war Alfa Romeos and Mercedes-Benz to Porsche 356 and Fiats, but also the crowds: half of the roads in Brescia are seemingly shut, and the rest thronged with people and cars. The famous red arrow flags are ubiquitous, and a Mille Miglia association gets you everywhere: even with our lowly “MEDIA” sticker, we were given a police motorcycle escort when the traffic blocked our path. John Mayhead The cars line up in order of their race number, roughly by age, and that’s important: the first cars leave at 11:30 a.m., then depart in groups of three every minute thereafter. If you’re one of the later cars, you still have the same 11-hour journey to complete; it’s a long day, and the other days can be even longer. We watched as the groups wished each other good luck, had photos taken with their cars, then finally climbed aboard. There was a sense I’ve only really felt one place before, at the forming-up area at the Goodwood Revival, where the noise of engines revving and the smell of high-octane gasoline is pervaded by a sense of nervous impatience. Then the time came: the cars were marshalled to a large digital clock, then released to the starting ramp, and set off on a journey that would last five days and 1200 miles. We watched them, first alongside in our car, then on the app that tracked them by GPS throughout the tour. I’m delighted to say that every one of the Manual Shift group and their cars completed the race, unlike 45 other competitors who were forced to retire and three who failed to reach the start line. John and Julie Herlihy achieved a phenomenal 37th place, made all the more impressive by their coefficient score of 1.60, giving them a significant scoring disadvantage compared to the 1.80-coefficient cars that inevitably dominated the top of the leaderboard. Bruce Roch, this time partnered by his younger son Logan, secured 87th place, a massive achievement for a team in a Jaguar XK with a coefficient of 1.40, but for everyone, the experience was almost as important as the result. Notable was the strong family element of the Manual Shift group, and the younger generation were well represented: As well as Logan and Bruce, Alisia Houghtaling drove with her mother Yulia, and Gabe Hrib Senior and Junior doubled up. Bruce and Logan Roche John Mayhead Clips on social media of the Mille Miglia inevitably show the glitz of the pre-start events, the glamour of the routes winding through the most beautiful parts of Italy, and the thrills and spills of the race, but the reality is still a true endurance event. This year, the weather swapped between sweltering heat and rain on days that often lasted 15 hours for the competitors, much longer for the Rizza Classic team who, while the competitors ate or slept, were often checking over the cars, trying to address problems before they developed into something more serious. When things did go wrong, the two van loads of spare parts were essential, as was all their mechanical experience, although they proved preparation was everything: other than a differential problem suffered by Hrib’s Jaguar that needed managing until the finish, the rest of the group’s cars completed the event with no serious issues. That’s not to say they didn’t earn their places at the finish: midway through the race, Ken Marlin messaged me, giving me an idea of the reality. “I am hot, tired and sleep deprived,” he said. “My hands hurt from holding the skinny steering wheel and if not for my gloves they would be blistered. The ball of my left foot hurts from so much clutch work; my left butt cheek and left thigh are cramping from the same. I have blisters forming on my right foot from the heel/toe required… But we are having an adventure.” John Mayhead John Mayhead Ken Marlin in his 1952 212/225S Sport Vignale Berlinetta John Mayhead It’s an addictive adventure, too. Next year, Marlin wants to try to break into the top 100 for the first time, and Houghtaling wants to double the size of the group to give more of the Manual Shift drivers the chance to take part. 2027 will be one hell of a good year to drive, too: it’s the 100th anniversary of the first race, 70 years since it was cancelled, and 50 since it was restored to its current form. Having been so close, I can totally understand why it is on so many people’s bucket lists, especially with a group of friends; this is gearhead nirvana. If I could do it, I would in a heartbeat. Blisters heal. Memories like this don’t fade. The post Behind the Daunting Preparation for the 2026 Mille Miglia appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: Freedom Holding Corp. Announces That It Has Completed an Offering of Its Common Stock
summary: Freedom Holding Corp. is a corporation organized in the United States under the laws of the State of Nevada and is the parent company of several operating subsidiaries primarily engaged in a broad range of activities in the securities…
body_text: Freedom Holding Corp. Announces That It Has Completed an Offering of Its Common Stock Download as PDF July 10, 2026 NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Freedom Holding Corp. (Nasdaq: FRHC), an international financial technology group, today announced that it has completed an offering of 2,374,356 shares of its common stock pursuant to Regulation S of the Securities Act of 1933 (the “ Securities Act ”), raising aggregate gross proceeds of nearly US$300 million. This announcement is not and does not form part of any offer or solicitation to purchase or subscribe for securities in the United States. The securities offered in the offering mentioned above will not be or have not been registered under the Securities Act and may not be offered or sold in the United States or to U.S. persons (other than distributors) absent registration or an applicable exemption from the registration requirements of the Securities Act. Hedging transactions involving the securities may not be conducted unless in compliance with the Securities Act.
